brief.head: Best minds behind bars
brief.text: There were periods, Amit Varma said, when a country’s finest intellectuals were not in universities, think tanks or air-conditioned cafes. “They were in jails.” {023-C03}

brief.head: Left, right, same game
brief.text: Labels like left and right hide what is really going on, Ajay Shah argued. Populism ignites hatred against elites, and whoever wields it, “at heart, it’s the same.” {023-C07}

brief.head: Chicken for the guest
brief.text: In Pashtun villages, Mukulika Banerjee found, beef was the staple, but every household kept an expensive chicken for honoured guests. To spare her hosts, she ate beef. {023-S04}

brief.head: The looking-glass self
brief.text: Amit Varma’s unwritten novel *Missing* has a student vanish from his hostel, and in a parallel strand everyone else vanishes. “If other people vanish, what is the self?” {023-C10}

brief.head: Sorry, Govindji
brief.text: Govind Nihalani once wanted to film Amit Varma’s novel *My Friend Sancho*. When it stalled, an embarrassed Varma stopped meeting him. On air, he apologised. {023-S17}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah play producer for a day
lead.head: Seven stories in want of a studio
body: Ajay Shah came out of Christopher Nolan’s *Dunkirk* feeling that a time machine had taken him back to 1940. {#dunkirk}
Why stop there, he asked. So many other scenes from history linger in the imagination that he and Amit Varma decided to hand a few to the people who make films.
The result was seven pitches for films and web series: four from Varma, three from Shah, with neither knowing the other’s list in advance.
The stories, Varma said, “also reveal a bit about us and the things that we care about”.
Shah predicted that Varma would one day become one of the world’s great movie makers. “You left me speechless for a moment,” Varma replied.
## Heroes of a kind
Varma, in a red kurta to honour the Red Shirts, opened with Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the Pathan whose Khudai Khidmatgar met every provocation with nonviolence.
Pakistan’s state crushed the movement after Partition. But when Bacha Khan died in 1988, a lonely old man, his memory still meant something to the common people. {023-S01}
Shah’s reply was a raid. At the airfield of Tatsinskaya, Soviet tanks sat at the edge of the runway and shot down the German transports supplying Stalingrad, one by one, as they took off. {023-S06}
Varma suggested that the real hero was somewhere in a back room, a thinker like Shah, planning the operation. “Of course,” Shah said, “no question.”
Varma’s second pitch was Haimabati Sen, married at nine to a widower of 45, widowed at ten, who made her way to Benares and became a doctor. {023-S08}
Shah followed with a theme rather than a tale: the bridges over which retreating German armies had to squeeze, and the military policemen who killed their own soldiers to keep order.
## The state against the citizen
The longest pitch was Varma’s web series on the Emergency, drawn from Coomi Kapoor’s book. It is dangerous to forget history, he said, because “it rhymes in disturbing ways”.

Its scenes would include a Haryana village besieged by police during the sterilisation drive, an actress jailed for her friendship with George Fernandes, and a headline the government could not stop: “Babu beats Bobby”.
Then a fiction. Varma’s *Missing* is a novel he once meant to write, about a student who vanishes from his hostel, and about a world in which, for that student, everyone else has vanished.
Shah revealed that his own parents’ elopement had once been optioned for a film.
## A title in wartime
Shah kept the last word for himself, with the story of how Arthur Koestler’s *Darkness at Noon* was written in Paris as France fell, nearly lost, and named by its translator, Daphne Hardy. {023-S20}
The book was really influential, Shah said. It changed the world, and in his telling it tipped the French election of 1946.
Varma closed by hoping some of the films would get made, so that the hosts could walk red carpets. Then he turned to Shah. “You couldn’t even wear a red shirt.”

second.label: Pitching the Emergency
second.head: A blockbuster backfires
second.deck: How a Doordarshan screening of Bobby failed to keep a rally empty
body: In 1977, as Amit Varma recalled it, the government was worried about a JP Narayan rally at which Jagjivan Ram was to speak. So it told Doordarshan to show *Bobby*, a huge hit of 1973, on the theory that everyone would stay home. {#bobby}
The rally was packed. Jagjivan Ram’s nickname was Babu, and the next day’s headline read “Babu beats Bobby”. {023-S14}

Varma would open his Emergency web series here: a portly, nervous politician putting on his cap backstage, intercut with a family huddled around a 1970s television set, watching Dimple Kapadia. The headline, he said, was the greatest in independent India’s history.

quote.text: And the headline in the newspaper the next day was Babu beats Bobby.

second.caption: the day Babu beat Bobby

third.head: Third time to Banaras
body: Amit Varma had just apologised on air for ghosting the filmmaker Govind Nihalani when Ajay Shah mentioned a production agreement of his own: his parents’ story had once been optioned.

They had an inter-caste marriage, and they eloped three times. “The first two times were terrible, violent events,” Shah said, “and then they ran and ran and did not stop running till they reached Banaras.” {023-S18}
There they married in secret, in an Arya Samaj ceremony. The film was never made.

Varma wanted to dig into it a little more, and could not resist a dig of his own. “And out of that great romantic, courageous affair emerges a boring card carrying economist,” he said. “What a waste. What a waste.” {023-J06}
third.caption: his parents’ elopement

p2.title: The pitch meeting
p2.deck: Four pitches from Amit Varma, three from Ajay Shah, and the ideas behind them

sections.label: Amit’s first
sections.head: Unarmed, and unafraid
sections.caption: the Servants of God
body: Amit Varma’s first pitch was a web series in two strands. One follows Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as Bacha Khan, whose Khudai Khidmatgar, the ‘servants of God’, grew from a thousand members in 1930 to lakhs of marchers in red kurtas. {#members}

The other follows Mukulika Banerjee, a PhD student in India in the late 1980s, who could not square his movement with academic convention. Peasants supposedly did not do mass politics; Pathans were supposedly a violent frontier people.
An adviser told her to do a PhD only if she had a question that kept her up at night. She had one. {023-S03}

For two years nobody would back a woman going to the North-West Frontier Province. When money came, partly from abroad, she learned Pashto, wore a chador and went from village to village looking for survivors. The book, *The Pathan Unarmed*, took ten years.
## Rooted at home

Her answer, which Varma read out, was that Bacha Khan built nonviolence from what his people already held: patience in Islam, the greater jihad against one’s own fear and anger, and the Pashtun codes of courage, hospitality and refuge. The British were unwanted guests, to be evicted “politely but firmly”. {023-C01}
~ The Pakistani state later crushed the movement. Yet when Bacha Khan died in 1988, Varma said, the common people still remembered. {023-S01}

quote.text: The state might have forgotten you and cast you away, but it still means something to the common people.

sections.label: Ajay’s first
sections.head: Hit them where they eat
sections.caption: the Soviet deep battle
body: Ajay Shah’s first pitch was set on the Eastern Front, where about 250,000 German troops were encircled at Stalingrad. Under normal conditions they needed 700 to 900 tons of supplies a day. {#tons}

Hitler’s team tried to keep them alive by air, as the Germans had done a year earlier for about 100,000 men near Leningrad. The bare survival minimum was 300 tons a day. What actually got through was 100 to 150. {#airlift}
## Choke the supply line

That made the airfields the target. Soviet doctrine, Shah said, is not to hit the enemy head on but to work out its logistics and hit those instead, the so-called deep battle. Ukraine, he noted, is doing the same to the Russian invaders today. {023-C04}

He added a point people rarely consider. Planes must be light, so many parts are made to wear out quickly. “It’s one thing to own a plane,” he said. “It’s a different thing for that plane to be airworthy.” {023-C05}
~ The correct level of human drama, Shah said, is *Dunkirk*’s: the events themselves are the grand drama. Amit Varma, no Christopher Nolan fanboy, called it the best war film ever made. {023-R16}

quote.text: You don’t hit the enemy, you figure out their logistics and you hit the logistics. You choke the logistics.

sections.label: Amit’s second
sections.head: A child widow’s long run
sections.caption: Haimabati Sen
body: Amit Varma’s second pitch opens in a sepia storeroom. A woman’s hand unlatches an old trunk and lifts out yellowed, half-torn papers. On a second soundtrack, a child’s feet run, stumble and fall. Then the credits.

The papers are the memoirs of Haimabati Sen, born in 1866 to a poor family in Khulna, then in Bengal and now in Bangladesh. At six, in the famine of 1872, she was caught stealing rice from the family store for the starving poor outside.
Her learning alarmed her elders, and at nine she was married to a 45-year-old widower with two children her own age. {#nine}

By twelve she was a destitute child widow, her money taken by an uncle. Many child widows, Varma said, ended up in prostitution. Haimabati went to Benares, educated herself and became a doctor. {023-S08}
## No path laid out
Varma first read about her in Kavitha Rao’s *Lady Doctors*. Every woman doctor of that century was remarkable, he said, because a man could arrive by inertia and a woman could not. {023-C11}
~ She began her memoirs in the 1920s and died in 1933. The papers lay in a trunk for eighty years, until Tapan Raychaudhuri convinced the family that they were a big deal. {023-S09}

quote.text: Why is this not a web series? Why is this not a film? What are you doing?

sections.label: Amit’s third
sections.head: The Emergency, in episodes
sections.caption: the Emergency
body: Amit Varma’s third pitch was a web series on the Emergency, drawn from Coomi Kapoor’s *The Emergency: A Personal History*. Everyone should read it, he said, to understand the oppressive power of the Indian state. {023-R11}
Its cast begins with Indira Gandhi. In a private letter to Sanjay in the late 1960s, which Kapoor reproduces, she essentially says that they care only about power, not left or right. {023-S10}

Then the side characters. Vidya Charan Shukla, as information and broadcasting minister, told Delhi’s editors: not one bad word against Indira Gandhi. Most complied. In LK Advani’s words, “when asked to bend, they chose to crawl.” {023-S11}
## Lives, not statistics

In Peepli, a Haryana village, an ageing widower died during a forced sterilisation. The village protested, police laid siege, and at 6 AM two women making cow-dung cakes outside were shot dead. {023-S12}
The actress Snehalata Reddy’s crime was friendship with George Fernandes, then on the run. Denied treatment for her asthma in jail, she died of a heart attack shortly after her release. {023-S13}

~ Many of today’s leaders were dissenters then. Had he been one, Varma said, he would have vowed to treat the opposition with dignity and let the press speak if he ever held power. He is not sure the lesson was learnt.

quote.text: The lesson I would take from this is how dangerous power is.

sections.label: Ajay’s last
sections.head: The book that swung France
sections.caption: the battle of ideas
body: Ajay Shah wanted his story to be the last word. It was about Arthur Koestler who, with George Orwell and Albert Camus, “lived at the dark crossroads of literature and politics”, in Lionel Trilling’s words.
*Darkness at Noon*, Shah said, goes inside the minds of the Soviet communist leaders who confessed to grotesque crimes in court. {023-R17}

Written in Paris as the Germans arrived, it survived by luck, and was titled by its translator, Daphne Hardy. Shah argued that it tipped the French election of 1946, which the Communist Party lost. {#french}
## The battle of ideas

Shah ranks Koestler and Orwell alongside Milton Friedman, Hayek and George Stigler in the 20th century’s battle between liberal democracy and authoritarian and populist philosophies. Many people, he said, have still not internalised its basics. {023-C12}

In 2015 the German manuscript turned up in Switzerland, and a new translation followed, informed by the briefly opened Kremlin archives. Shah held up his two most prized possessions: a 1941 edition that came from his father, and the 2015 one. {023-S21}
~ Amit Varma answered with Stefan Zweig’s *The World of Yesterday*, reading its lament that “all the pale horses of the apocalypse have stormed through my life”. {023-R18}

quote.text: Dear reader, I commend you please read these books, and you know what? Read both versions.

side.boxText: Gandhi first saw in Bacha Khan a kindred soul, then an inspiration, and once called his movement the practical form of the nonviolence he believed in. Amit Varma reads its ‘God’ as a set of higher principles. {023-J14}

contQuote.text: India contains multitudes. India contains the opposite values. Our culture can cater to the worst of our instincts, but it can also cater to the best of our instincts.

p3.title: Scenes to shoot
p3.deck: Four stories from the episode, and what each one teaches

stories.start: So all of us know that story, that two hundred and fifty thousand people
stories.end: just shattered, and then weeks later, uh Paulus uh surrendered
stories.caption: the raid on Tatsinskaya
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s Eastern Front epic, set on a single airfield
stories.head: Tanks at the edge of the runway
body: The airfield at Tatsinskaya was the closest to the action. About 200 German planes were based there, flying supplies to the army trapped inside Stalingrad, and Ajay Shah’s film would be set on its runway.
Each transport carried about 2.5 tons on a sortie of an hour and a half: think Bombay to Delhi, or Bombay to Bhopal, Shah said. It unloaded, took on wounded men and flew back, again and again.

Soviet intelligence knew what the airfield was for, though it lay about 80 km inside German-held territory. In an almost suicidal operation, a group of tanks and soldiers punched through the thin German lines and headed for it. The surprise was complete: the scouts raised the alarm only ten minutes before the T-34s arrived. {#ten}
Pandemonium followed. Planes with too little fuel tried to take off at once, and many crashed into each other, under artillery and tank fire.

Then came what Shah called one of the most priceless fragments of the story. T-34s parked at the edge of the runway, aimed, and waited. As each plane lifted off, a tank shell, flying more or less straight, blew it up. “The tanks were like fat frogs grabbing one drone ant at a time,” he said. {023-S06}
By Shah’s memory, about 70 planes were destroyed and about 130 got away. {#seventy}
~ The survivors had to fly from a farther airfield, making longer trips with fewer planes. The supply of the Sixth Army was shattered. Weeks later, Paulus surrendered. {#paulus}
stories.why: Big things often hinge on little things, Amit Varma said, and this raid is at once a microcosm and a macrocosm of the war. The heroes, the hosts agreed, are the planners in a back room, working out the logistics.
stories.postscript: Varma preferred this use of “fat frogs”. The last time Shah used the phrase, he said, it was to tell Varma to lose weight. {023-J05}

stories.start: this concerns river crossings. Okay, so once again we are back in
stories.end: used as a lovely backdrop in which a beautiful movie can be
stories.caption: the river crossings
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a scene that played out about ten times
stories.head: Shot by their own side
body: The Red Army covered about 2,500 km from Stalingrad to Berlin in about 500 days, Ajay Shah said: the distance from Ludhiana to Kanyakumari. {#berlin}

About ten times along the way, a retreating German army, with its men, equipment and stores, had to cross a river by a single bridge. Artillery was too imprecise to destroy such bridges easily, so they held. But every crossing was an operations problem: what to leave behind, and how many vehicles of what kind could get across in a day.
Tired, scared men tended to break ranks, and a mob wrecks a crossing. At several of these crossings, the German military police killed German soldiers to hold the discipline. {023-S07}
~ Shah reached for fluid mechanics. “What you want is a laminar flow and not a turbulent flow,” he said. {023-C06}

quote.text: So think of each bridge as a choke point where there is a trapped army and its equipment and its stores.

stories.start: There is a story about how Virindir Kapoor was imprisoned.
stories.end: getting into the train and there's a crowd there to see him off
stories.caption: a note dropped from a prison van
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a stranger’s kindness in the Emergency
stories.head: A note falls from a van
body: During the Emergency, the journalist Virendra Kapoor, Coomi Kapoor’s husband, was moved between jails in a police van. He wanted her to know which station he would be at, Amit Varma said, so that she could see him.

He scribbled a parchi with her landline number and dropped it out of the back. A man on a scooter behind the van saw it fall, waited until the van was out of sight, picked it up and got the message to her. {#parchi}
She went to Bareilly to see him and three other prisoners put on a train, not knowing if she would see him again.
~ “And at the same time, and the scene is so cinematic,” Varma said, a crowd at the other end of the platform was chanting slogans for a Congress politician boarding the same train. {023-S15}
stories.why: Under repression, small acts of decency by strangers kept people connected. In the same frame, a few metres away, the powerful went on celebrating, which is what made the scene, to Varma, so cinematic.

stories.start: Now at the time, uh so Koesler was Hungarian and his native language was German.
stories.end: And put it in a post box to his book editor in Switzerland.
stories.caption: the writing of Darkness at Noon
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a world-changing novel nearly vanished
stories.head: Page by page, as Paris fell
body: In 1940 Arthur Koestler, a Hungarian who wrote in German, was living in a dingy part of Paris with his girlfriend, Daphne Hardy, a 21-year-old British art student. He wrote *Darkness at Noon* page by page, Ajay Shah said, and she translated each page into English.
Her German was not so good, and she knew little of Soviet Russia. So an interrogation, in her English, became a hearing. {#interrogation}
Then the Germans reached Paris and France surrendered. Koestler, a wanted man, was interned. “The only reason he got away was because of bad identity infrastructure,” Shah said. {023-S19}

~ Before they parted, he posted the German manuscript to his editor in Switzerland. Hardy hid the dangerous English one and was evacuated from Marseille. Koestler escaped, Shah thinks by walking across the Pyrenees into Spain.
stories.why: A book that changed the world nearly never reached it. Its survival hung on luck, on Hardy’s courage, and on German officials who never worked out whom they had interned.
stories.postscript: Shah’s advice to fans of digital identity: “Think twice.” {023-J10}

quiz.q: What did Mukulika Banerjee’s adviser say was the only reason to do a PhD?
quiz.a: A question that keeps you up at night, which you are desperate to answer.

quiz.q: Why, by Ajay Shah’s account, did the airlift to Stalingrad collapse after the Tatsinskaya raid?
quiz.a: With about 70 planes lost, survivors flew longer trips from a farther airfield.

quiz.q: What did the Akali prisoners do when British jailers ordered them to remove their turbans?
quiz.a: They stripped to their underwear and kept only their turbans on.

quiz.q: What film did Doordarshan show to keep people away from Jagjivan Ram’s rally?
quiz.a: *Bobby*, the 1973 hit. The rally was packed anyway: Babu beats Bobby.

quiz.q: What fluid mechanics analogy did Ajay Shah use for an army crossing a bridge?
quiz.a: Laminar flow, not turbulent: a smooth, planned crossing, not a panicking mob.

quiz.q: Who chose the title *Darkness at Noon*, and what had Koestler called his book?
quiz.a: Daphne Hardy, his translator. His working title was *Rubashov: A Novel*.
